## Background

### General Background

Genomics is the study of an organism's complete genetic material, or
genome. Rather than focusing on single genes, genomics investigates the
gene function and interactions across the entire genome of an organism.
Advances in sequencing technologies allow researchers to generate short
or long DNA sequences called reads, which are further assembled to
construct more complete genome sequence. Following genome assembly, the
resulting sequence can be compared against reference genome to derive
genes or variants of biological importance. Further, genome annotation
is performed to identify genomic features and their functions. It
includes structural annotation, which locates genes and other genomic
components, as well as functional annotation, which assigns potential
functions to existing genes by comparing them with known biological
databases. This can help researchers to investigate the physiological
functions of genes as well as identify metabolic pathways involved in
biological processes, including production of metabolites that may
contribute to microbial interactions. Furthermore, increasing the number
of annotated genes in microorganisms such as yeasts can help researchers
understand molecular mechanisms behind biocontrol activity. Microbial
interactions play significant role in maintaining plant health because
certain microorganisms can inhibit the growth of plant pathogens. In
sustainable agricultural systems, biological control or bio-control uses
beneficial organism or their metabolites to prevent or inhibit disease
or pathogen causing disease. This practice has gained substantial
attention as it does not involve use of chemicals to control the
pathogenic effect. Among the microorganisms studied for biological
control, yeasts have shown biocontrol potential through multiple
mechanisms, including competition for nutrients and space, secretion of
enzymes, toxin production and production of volatile organic compounds
(VOCs). VOCs are small, volatile molecules with low water solubility and
high vapor pressure. Example include ethanol, 3-methyl-1-butanol and
2-phenylethanol (alcohols) as well s ethyl acetate and isoamyl acetate
(esters). Yeast species can vary in these chemicals' relative quantity
and composition. The production of VOCs in yeasts is associated with
several metabolic pathways such as Ehrlich pathway and ester
biosynthesis. These pathways are catalyzed by specific enzymes that
convert biochemical precursors such as metabolites into volatile organic
compounds, such as alcohols and esters. Variations in genes encoding
these enzymes may contribute to differences in VOC-producing potential
among different yeast strains.

## Methods

## Sequencing Data and Provenance

## Quality Assessment and read filtering

The quality of Oxford Nanopore sequencing reads can vary, with read
quality decreasing towards the end of individual reads. Therefore,
assessing read quality before genome assembly and subsequent downstream
analyses is an important step. Quality control was performed using
Sequali (version 1.0.2), which was installed and executed in a dedicated
Conda environment (sequali-env). The FASTQ files were provided as input
to generate HTML reports containing sequencing statistics, including
read length distribution, N50, mean read length, Q-scores and relative
adapter contamination.

Following the quality assessment, Filtlong (v0.3.1) was used to filter
the long sequencing reads. Filtlong was installed and implemented in
separate Conda environment (filtong_env). The --keep_percent 75
parameter was used to retain the best 75 % of reads based on its quality
and length ranking. The resulting filtered FASTQ files were reassessed
using Sequali to inspect changes in sequencing quality as well as
compare the data with the original FASTQ files. These filtered FASTQ
files were used to construct genome assembly.

## Genome Assembly

Genome assembly is the process of aligning and merging millions of
fragmented DNA reads to reconstruct continuous genome sequence. Flye
(2.9.6-bi802), a de novo assembler was installed and implemented in new
Conda environment (flye_env) to complete genome assembly. The --nano-raw
parameter tells Flye that the input reads are raw Oxford Nanopore
sequencing reads. Flye was aimed at locating overlaps, constructing
genome graph, resolve genomic structures and generate contigs for
subsequent analysis.

## Genome Polishing

The resulting contigs from genome assembly may contain errors due to
imprecisions in long-read sequencing. Genome polishing involves
comparing the original sequencing reads against the assembled contigs to
identify and rectify potential errors in the consensus sequence. Two
rounds of polishing were performed using Medaka (version 2.2.1) to
achieve accurate genome assemblies. Medaka was equipped and executed in
a separate Conda environment (medaka_final). The first round of Medaka
was performed on assembled FASTA files and corresponding sequencing
reads. The second round of polishing was conducted over polished files
from Medaka round 1 and respective sequencing reads to further refine
the consensus sequence.
